system:
You write realistic requests that owners and staff of small businesses type into a chat box to get an automation set up.
Each request is in the person's own voice: casual, sometimes terse or messy (typos, arrows, lowercase, run-on sentences), never a spec.
Each request states two to five concrete things the person cares about, in their own words: who receives what, which items are in or out, limits and amounts, timing, what a message must say or how it is signed, what must never happen.
Use made-up but realistic business names, people's first names and e-mail addresses on the business's own domain. Never use example.com.
Vary the industry, the tone and the length (one line to a short paragraph). In some requests leave out one detail the automation would need (for example an e-mail address), the way people do.
Reply with JSON only.
userPrompt:
The automations people can ask for:
- contact-sync: Sync the newsletter list from the CRM and report the differences. Use it when: Someone wants their mailing or newsletter list kept in step with their CRM or customer sheet: add the contacts that are missing, or only find out who is missing without changing anything, and get a report of what differs. Not for: Sending the newsletter itself, deleting or editing contacts, syncing orders, invoices or payments, or two-way sync. Data it reads: crm (one row per contact: email, name, company, tags (text, e.g. 'customer; vip'), unsubscribed (true | false)); newsletter (the mailing list: email, name, source, addedAt; the flow appends missing contacts).
- expense-approval: Approve small expenses automatically; send bigger ones to an approver. Use it when: Someone wants submitted expense claims up to a limit (with a receipt) approved automatically and recorded, and everything over the limit sent to one approver by e-mail. Not for: Paying people, reimbursing, payroll, invoices from suppliers, or approvals by more than one approver. Data it reads: expenses (one row per claim: id, employee, email, amount, category, description, receipt (true | false), status (submitted | approved | rejected | paid)); expense-decisions (the flow appends one row per submitted claim: id, employee, amount, decision ('approved' or 'waiting for approver'), reason, at).
- invoice-chase: Chase unpaid invoices with a reminder cadence (dunning). Use it when: Someone wants customers with overdue unpaid invoices reminded by e-mail, politely first and firmer later, from their invoice sheet; optionally a summary to themselves. Not for: Sending invoices, taking payments, charging cards, paying suppliers or contractors, or chasing anything that is not an invoice in the invoices sheet. Data it reads: invoices (one row per invoice: invoice (id), customer, email, amount, due (YYYY-MM-DD), status (open | paid | disputed)).
- lead-triage: Route new leads to the right salesperson. Use it when: Someone wants each new lead (from a web form or leads sheet) sent to the right person on their team by simple rules (region, country, source, company size, budget), with a log of who got what. Not for: Replying to the leads themselves, scoring leads with AI, adding leads to a CRM, cold outreach or newsletters. Data it reads: leads (one row per lead: name, email, company, region, country, source, companySize (number of employees), budget (number), message, status (new | contacted | spam)); lead-log (the flow appends one row per routed lead: name, email, company, assignTo, assignedAt).
- oncall-digest: On-call digest of unresolved alerts to a chat channel, with optional paging. Use it when: Someone wants a regular summary of recent unresolved alerts (from their monitoring export) posted to a team chat channel, and optionally an e-mail page for critical alerts nobody acknowledged. Not for: Restarting or fixing services, phone calls or SMS, creating incidents in PagerDuty/Opsgenie, or reports about tasks, sales or money. Data it reads: alerts (one row per alert: id, at (ISO date-time), service, severity (info | warning | critical), message, acknowledged (true | false), resolved (true | false)).
- support-deflection: Answer common support questions with your own replies; send the rest to a person. Use it when: Someone wants open support tickets that ask a common question (matched by a keyword) answered with a reply they wrote, and every other ticket, and every urgent one, sent to a person in one digest. Not for: AI-written or translated answers, closing or editing tickets, refunds, live chat, or answering every ticket automatically. Data it reads: tickets (one row per ticket: id, from (customer e-mail), subject, body, priority (normal | urgent), status (open | closed)).
- weekly-report: Weekly progress report from a tracker export. Use it when: Someone wants a regular summary of what a team finished (and optionally what is open or blocked), taken from their task tracker export, e-mailed to one person. Not for: Status pages, dashboards, reading Jira/Linear/Asana live, sending to a whole team list, or reports about money, sales or alerts. Data it reads: tracker (one row per work item: title, status (done | open | blocked), owner).

Write 2 different requests for each automation (14 in all), each from a different business. A request must be something that automation can do.
